q: What is the unit of activity?
a: The becquerel (Bq): one decay per second.

q: Where are protons and neutrons found?
a: In the nucleus.

q: What are the relative charges of proton, neutron and electron?
What is the atomic (proton) number Z?
a: The number of protons in the nucleus.

q: What is the mass (nucleon) number A?
a: The number of protons plus neutrons.

q: How do you find the number of neutrons?
a: A − Z.

q: How many neutrons are in ¹⁴₆C?
Why is a neutral atom neutral?
a: Number of electrons = number of protons.

q: What is an isotope?
a: Atoms of the same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons (different A).

q: How many neutrons in U-235 and U-238?
What does ‘random’ mean for decay?
a: We cannot predict which nucleus will decay or when.

q: What does ‘ionising’ mean?
a: The radiation knocks electrons off atoms.

q: What is an alpha particle?
a: A helium nucleus: 2 protons + 2 neutrons (charge +2).

q: What is a beta (β⁻) particle?
a: A fast electron from the nucleus (charge −1).

q: What is gamma radiation?
a: An electromagnetic wave with no charge or mass.

q: Which radiation is most ionising?
a: Alpha.

q: Which radiation is most penetrating?
a: Gamma.

q: What stops alpha radiation?
a: A sheet of paper (or a few cm of air).

q: What stops beta radiation?
a: A few mm of aluminium.

q: What reduces gamma radiation?
a: Thick lead or concrete.

q: Name two detectors of radiation.
a: Photographic film and a Geiger–Müller (GM) tube.

q: How does a film badge work?
a: Radiation fogs the film; more fogging means more radiation received.

q: Penetration practical: what must stay the same? (8.6)
a: The distance from source to detector and the counting time.

q: Why measure the background count?
a: So it can be subtracted to find the count from the source.

q: Name sources of background radiation.
a: Radon and rocks, food, building materials, cosmic rays, medical sources.

q: Effect of alpha emission on A and Z?
a: A decreases by 4; Z decreases by 2.

q: Effect of beta (β⁻) emission on A and Z?
a: A stays the same; Z increases by 1.

q: Effect of gamma emission on A and Z?
a: No change.

q: Effect of neutron emission on A and Z?
a: A decreases by 1; Z stays the same.

q: What must balance in a nuclear equation?
a: Mass numbers (top) and charges / atomic numbers (bottom).

q: Complete: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ?
a: ⁴₂He (an alpha particle).

q: Complete: ²⁴₁₁Na → ²⁴₁₂Mg + ?
a: ⁰₋₁e (a beta particle).

q: ²³⁴₉₀Th → ²³⁴ₓPa + ⁰₋₁e. Find x.
Which symbols are accepted for the electron in beta decay?
a: β, β⁻, e, e⁻ (not β⁺).

q: What happens to activity over time?
a: It decreases.

q: Define half-life.
a: The time taken for the activity (or number of undecayed nuclei) to halve.

q: Is ‘half the time’ a correct definition?
a: No: it scores no marks.

q: Do all isotopes have the same half-life?
a: No: it is different for different isotopes.

q: What fraction is left after 3 half-lives?
a: One eighth.

q: How do you find the number of half-lives?
a: Total time ÷ half-life.

q: 640 Bq, half-life 5 min. Activity after 20 min?
960 Bq → 120 Bq in 45 min. Half-life?
a: 3 halvings: 45 ÷ 3 = 15 min.

q: How do you read half-life from a graph?
a: Pick an activity, find half of it, read the time difference.

q: What do you do about background in half-life questions?
a: Subtract it first; add it back if the measured count is asked for.

q: Which radiation is used as a medical tracer?
a: Gamma, with a short half-life.

q: Why must a tracer have a short half-life?
a: Its activity falls quickly so the patient receives less radiation.

q: Which radiation treats cancer?
a: Beta (or alpha): short range, kills nearby cells.

q: Which radiation sterilises instruments?
a: Gamma: it penetrates the packaging and kills bacteria.

q: Which radiation controls paper thickness?
a: Beta.

q: What is irradiation?
a: Exposure to radiation from a source outside the object.

q: What is contamination?
a: Radioactive material on or inside an object or person.

q: Does irradiation make an object radioactive?
a: No.

q: What are two dangers of ionising radiation?
a: It damages cells and tissue, and causes mutations (cancer).

q: Name two ways to reduce the risk from a source.
a: Shielding, distance (tongs), short exposure time.

q: How is radioactive waste stored?
a: In sealed lead or concrete containers, vitrified, underground.

q: What starts fission of U-235?
a: A neutron hitting the nucleus.

q: What does fission of U-235 produce?
a: Two radioactive daughter nuclei, 2 or 3 neutrons and energy.

q: In what form is the energy released?
a: Kinetic energy of the fission products.

q: What is a chain reaction?
a: Neutrons from one fission cause further fissions.

q: When is a chain reaction uncontrolled?
a: When each fission causes more than one further fission.

q: What does the moderator do?
a: Slows the neutrons so they are more easily absorbed by U-235.

q: What do the control rods do?
a: Absorb neutrons, decreasing the rate of fission.

q: How is the rate kept constant?
a: By changing the position of the control rods.

q: Why is a reactor surrounded by thick concrete?
a: It absorbs radiation to protect workers and the environment.

q: What is nuclear fusion?
a: Small nuclei join to form a larger nucleus, releasing energy.

q: What happens to mass in fusion?
a: The new nucleus has less mass; the loss is released as energy.

q: What is the energy source of stars?
a: Fusion.

q: Complete: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ?
a: ¹₀n (a neutron).

q: Why does fusion need very high temperature?
a: To give nuclei enough speed to overcome their repulsion.

q: Why are nuclei repelling each other?
a: They are positively charged (protons): electrostatic repulsion.

q: Why are there no fusion power plants?
a: Needs high temperature/pressure; cannot be sustained or run commercially; needs a large energy input.

q: One difference between fission and fusion?
a: Fission splits a large nucleus; fusion joins small nuclei.
